newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Holzmann finances and orders improve.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Holzmann finances and orders improve.

text.p: Troubled German construction group Philipp Holzmann AG on Tuesday said its financial situation had improved and it aimed to restore loss-making operations to profit by next year.

Holzmann reported that 1996 construction output was steady at 14.1 billion marks ($8.3 billion) and the cornerstone for its "pleasing results" was an improvement in new orders and its foreign business against a backdrop of a sluggish German economy and increased competition.
"The financial situation at Philipp Holzmann has clearly improved in previous months. Holzmann will continue its determined restructuring programme in 1997," the group said in a statement.
Incoming orders last year were 16.5 billion marks, a rise of 7.6 percent, while orders in hand grew by 20.8 percent to 15.9 billion.
The group reported a sharp improvement in liquid assets and securities to 2.6 billion marks in 1996 from 1.7 billion.
The performance exceeded industry analysts' hopes and the group's shares rose nine marks to 460 soon after the figures were announced, closing up eight at 459.

Uwe Weinrich, construction analyst at BHF Bank, said: "These results are better than we had expected and levels of confidence in Holzmann are on the rise. I had been expecting foreign orders to grow by around 8.5 percent but they grew by 10.9 percent instead."

"I was really convinced by Holzmann's North American story -- the U.S. was very strong with 9.3 percent growth, which is important as Holzmann has the highest construction output abroad in absolute terms of the German construction companies," said Weinrich.
As well as strong growth in the United States, Holzmann said its construction output in Thailand grew by 35.5 percent.
The state of the domestic construction industry means that growth in foreign markets is vital for Holzmann.
Germany's construction industry is mired in pessimism because of the weak outlook for demand and prices in the domestic market, where infrastructure investment is falling.
Domestic incoming orders for Holzmann fell 5.3 percent to 9.2 billion marks. Of this, orders in the former east Germany dropped by 11.8 percent to 3.7 billion marks.
Weinrich is forecasting an overall operating loss for 1996 of 450 million marks but this is considerably less than previously anticipated for Holzmann.
Last month Holzmann denied reports that it made an operating loss of 600 million marks in 1996, up from a loss of 385 million in 1995, and said the estimate was too high.
The forecast operating loss takes into account charges of one billion marks resulting from writedowns on share stakes, operating losses and provisions.

The group said that it would seek to cut personnel and administration costs and the introduction of programmes aimed at optimising purchasing, financial and risk management would also lead to lower costs.
"All of these measures will build upon the solid foundation of high orders in hand to lead to higher earnings," Holzmann said.
Weinrich said: "We liked the fact that Holzmann says it is not planning to sell its loss-making units but has the confidence to say they will be turned into profitable subsidiaries."
